appraisal_events.evidence: « Mais dans mon imagination maintenant, Albertine était libre, elle usait mal de cette liberté, elle se prostituait aux unes, aux autres » ; le souvenir du peignoir de douche et « les deux jeunes filles amies de Léa » qui allaient à l’établissement balnéaire « pas seulement pour prendre des douches » ; « Ne pourrais-je pas du moins tâcher de savoir si Albertine n’avait jamais rien fait de mal dans cet établissement de douches ? »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator's posthumous jealousy converts Albertine into a permanent « coupable » — imagined prostituting herself, retroactively suspected through her blush and through the compromising company of Léa's friends, and made the object of a planned inquiry at Balbec. The narration stages this degradation while simultaneously undercutting it, presenting the accusation as a mechanism of memory and jealousy (« pour la jalousie il n’est ni passé ni avenir ») rather than as an established fact.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Je n’étais pas un seul homme, mais le défilé heure par heure d’une armée compacte où il y avait, selon le moment, des passionnés, des indifférents, des jaloux » ; « un jaloux lamentable et toujours contemporain » ; « comme aux amputés, le moindre changement de temps renouvelait mes douleurs dans le membre qui n’existait plus »
appraisal_events.explanation: The passage's dominant body diminishes the narrator himself: dispersed into a crowd of successive selves, unable to act on a past that functions as a crueler future, and explicitly labelled « lamentable » in his jealousy. The self-analysis is the narrated point and is carried without ironic distance.

status_effects.explanation: He is locally at his weakest: suffering renewed by every change of weather, powerless before Albertine's past, and self-described as a lamentable jealous man with no possibility of acting on what torments him.

Within the narrator's imagination she is degraded into a promiscuous and guilty figure whose faults are to be investigated now that she cannot retaliate; the narrator's own critique of his jealousy keeps the local drop moderate.
Dead, she nonetheless retains total leverage over the narrator — « si vivante en moi », resurrected at will, governing his suffering and making the eventual cure something he does not even wish for.

ambiguities: The stance on the accusation against Albertine is layered: the narrator vividly enacts the suspicion (prostitution, the douches inquiry, Léa's friends) while explicitly diagnosing it as a contradiction and an artefact of jealousy's abolished chronology, so the text neither establishes her guilt nor withdraws the imagined charge.
